messages.subject: Integrated approach results
parts:
I thought I would start a new thread as previous ones have got a bit long and off topic.

I have an algorithm which integrates NUTS, DREAM, and BFGS.

I present some initial results for a 64 dimensional highly anisotropic normal function.

In all cases, except where noted, I use about 100,000 function/derivative calculations. That is about the limit which is realistcally possible on my 'real' problem.

I use a burn-in of 10% of the total steps.

I calculate the mean and variance for the correlated direction. The analytical solution is mean 0.0, variance 10.0.

The results are very promising, but this is not surprising as the Hessian is constant. I will do some similar tests for Rosenbrock, where initial tests have shown a less clear picture, but I also want to find something for which there is an analytical solution to the cdf.....

This will be about the limit of my reporting results for this normal function - I will not be doing any more tuning or analysis of any more diagnostics, as I have other priorities.

messages.author: ace57905b77e39eb
messages.subject: Re: Integrated approach results
parts:
Here are some results for Rosenbrock. 64 dimensions.

I do the integration:

INTEGRATE[R exp(-R)]

i.e. my log likelihood is rosenbrock, and I am integration a function rosenbrock.

I don't think this has any analytical solution - if anybody can suggest an integration of the form:

INTEGRATE[f exp(-R)]

as a test case, I would be very grateful...

My results are below. As I say, much less clear situation. The amount of burn-in is clearly important, and the use of BFGS is less productive. This is easy to understand in such a complex multi modal situation. i do not use a changing Hessian during leapfrogs a la Riemann paper.

Both NUTS and NUTS+DREAM+BFGS settle on a mean of about 34 - 40, but a wider range in variance of about 40 - 80. Of course, there is a danger that all the methods get stuck in a local minimum and report a variance which is too small.

My starting points are normally distributed, mean zero variance one.

In my 'real' problem I would start off with much better starting values, using different methods. I am sure that problem with a long burn-in being needed is because of poor starting points, but I am trying to expose rather than hide problems.

I report the mean and variance, and the best value found for the Rosenbrock.

Some more Rosenbrock results. DREAM with parallel tempering (PT) and a basic HMC with PT.

HMC with PT seems to confirm the best of previous results, which is encouraging, as PT should help multi modes.

DREAM, with or without PT, gives a consistently higher mean.

Who knows which is 'correct'!

Although DREAM, by itself, does not do very well compared with NUTS on the anisotropic normal case.

But that doesn't mean that DREAM does not do better in a multi modal situation.

You will see in these results classic cases where repeatability does NOT show convergence.

I haven't yet implemented NUTS + PT, and probably won't do so.

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Integrated approach results
parts:
Is your BFGS method based on Zhang and Sutton's algorithm? It's not
clear to me that there's any good (non-Riemannian) alternative to that
approach that preserves detailed balance.

If you are doing something along those lines, then these results make
perfect sense. The Zhang and Sutton method is great, but (like DREAM,
and unlike RMHMC) it can only use global curvature information. The
Rosenbrock function's curvature varies wildly depending on your
location, so it's not surprising that there's no single Hessian that
gives huge performance gains. The multivariate normal, on the other
hand, has constant curvature, so this ceases to be an issue.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Integrated approach results
parts:
No, I'm not doing anything like Zhang and Sutton.

I'm pretty sure I'm maintaining detailed balance.

I am using both NUTS and DREAM in a single scheme.

But your analysis is correct - I am using a 'global' Hessian, rather than changing it along leapfrogs, so there are obvious limitations for Rosenbrock. It would be different if all the chains were converging to the same mode.

Interestingly enough, when I try to change it along leapfrogs, or when calculating an initial epsilon, it very quickly starts exploding and showing numerical problems with very long steps. So it isn't just detailed balance which is thrown, the whole thing becomes unstable.

The choices on the changes in theta and changes in gradient, for input to updating the Hessian, are a particular set I have chosen, and there may be alternatives which maintain balance and are better for improving the NUTS aspects of the integrated algorithm - i.e. are a better 'local' approximation.

Whether my 'real' problem is as difficult as Rosenbrock I will see in the next day or two.

Sorry for teasing - if you want to know more, contact me by email.

At least my results so far show that there is a class of problems for which my integrated approach seems to perform significantly better than NUTS.
